problem: How to interpret the paper's finding that the AD transformer improves in-context on held-out Dark Room tasks, which could indicate a general RL algorithm or a simpler mechanism.
did: Interpreted the AD agent as implementing a simple heuristic (move to where the previous episode ended in reward 1, otherwise move pseudorandomly) rather than a general-purpose RL algorithm.
alternatives_named: AD agent implements a reasonably general RL algorithm / is a mesa-optimizer
stated_reason: Once the input contains an episode ending in reward 1, the model can directly infer the goal location, so no general planning or exploration-exploitation balancing is needed.
quote: it suffices to implement the much simpler heuristic "if your input contains an episode ending in reward 1, then move towards the position the agent was in at the end of that episode; otherwise, move around pseudorandomly."
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: How to judge whether the training and deployment tasks in the paper are genuinely different, which determines whether generalization to them demonstrates a general algorithm.
did: Argued that tasks differing only in goal location should not count as different under a reasonable notion of task.
alternatives_named: counting each goal location as a distinct task, as the paper does
stated_reason: The training tasks are extremely similar to each other and to the deployment task, so they only count as different under a pathologically narrow notion of task.
quote: First the training tasks used in this paper are all *extremely* similar to each other and to the deployment task; in fact, I think they only ought to count as *different* under a pathologically narrow notion of "task."
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: Which experiments to scrutinize when assessing the paper's claims.
did: Focused the analysis on the Dark Room family of experiments, claiming the critique generalizes to the paper's other experiments.
alternatives_named: analyzing all experiments in the paper individually
stated_reason: Concreteness; the author says the complaint applies equally to the other experiments.
quote: For concreteness, I'll focus here on one family of experiments, Dark Room, that appeared in the paper, but my complaint applies just as well to the other experiments in the paper.
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: What evidence would convincingly show that AD learns a general RL algorithm rather than a narrow heuristic.
did: Specified that in-context learning of a non-trivially different task (e.g. keys and boxes) after Dark Room training would count as strong evidence of a mesa-optimizer.
stated_reason: Such a task would not be solvable by the simple 'navigate to a fixed grid position' heuristic.
quote: If the AD agent trained in this paper were able to learn to do any non-trivially different task (e.g. an AD agent trained on Dark Room tasks were able to in-context learn a task involving collecting keys and unlocking boxes), then I would take that as strong evidence
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: Whether AD outperforming expert distillation (ED) refutes the simple-heuristic interpretation.
did: Declined to treat the ED vs AD gap as strong evidence against his interpretation, explaining it via uninformative rewards in expert data.
alternatives_named: treating ED's failure as evidence that AD learns a real RL algorithm
stated_reason: ED training data has every episode ending in reward 1, so ED cannot learn to respond differently to different rewards.
quote: The result is that the rewards in these training data are *very uninformative* \-\- every episode ends with reward 1 and no episodes end with a 0, so there's no chance for the ED agents to learn to respond differently to different rewards.
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: How to interpret the authors' explanation that ED fails because it cannot explore while AD can.
did: Agreed that AD explores but interpreted its exploration as mimicking an incompetent RL agent rather than sophisticated exploration.
alternatives_named: AD performing sophisticated exploration as part of a general RL algorithm
stated_reason: Under his heuristic account, AD simply imitates incompetent early-training agents when it does not know the goal.
quote: But the sort of exploration that the AD agent does is likely "when you don't know what to do, mimic an incompetent RL agent" rather than some more sophisticated exploration as part of a general RL algorithm.
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: How strongly to state the claim about what the AD agents actually learned, given the lack of direct verification.
did: Hedged the claim with phrases like 'strongly suspect' and conceded the agent may have learned a few additional heuristics, while still denying mesa-optimizer status.
stated_reason: The sum total of such heuristics is unlikely to be sophisticated enough to count as a mesa-optimizer.
quote: Well, probably the AD agent learned a few other interesting heuristics, like "if the last episode *didn't* end by reaching the goal position, then navigate to different part of the environment," but I'd be surprised if the sum total
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: What the ED agents do at deployment given they fail to improve, with no direct data in the paper to settle it.
did: Guessed that ED agents pick one goal position from training and repeatedly navigate there, rather than claiming a verified mechanism.
stated_reason: This fits the flat or degraded ED performance the authors describe.
quote: In fact, I'd guess that ED agents tend to pick some particular goal position from their training data and iteratively navigate to that goal position, never incurring reward so long as the deployment goal position isn't along the path
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: Whether the prediction markets' top-tier score can be accepted as evidence that markets beat other aggregation methods, given unequal research time.
did: They declined to treat the market victory as evidence of superiority and planned a fairer test with participants who do more research next year.
alternatives_named: accept that prediction markets are better than other aggregation methods
stated_reason: Contest participants had at most five minutes of research per question while market participants could spend as long as they wanted, so the comparison is unfair.
quote: That means prediction markets’ victory doesn’t necessarily mean they’re better than other aggregation methods - it might just mean that people who can do lots of research beat people who do less research.
title: [Crosspost] ACX 2022 Prediction Contest Results

problem: How to interpret the top individual forecaster's score of 25.68 among 508 entrants.
did: They attributed the result to a combination of skill and luck rather than concluding he was better than aggregates and markets.
alternatives_named: he is smarter than aggregates and prediction markets
stated_reason: With 508 entries there were 508 chances to outperform the markets by coincidence.
quote: There were 508 entries, ie 508 lottery tickets to outperform the markets by coincidence. Most likely he won by a combination of skill and luck.
title: [Crosspost] ACX 2022 Prediction Contest Results

problem: How to compare prediction markets fairly with participants' forecasts when markets covered only some questions.
did: They restricted the headline graph and scores to the 61 of 71 questions that had market estimates, adding the other ten back before awarding prizes.
alternatives_named: use all 71 questions for the comparison
stated_reason: To keep the prediction market results commensurable with the other results.
quote: This number and the following graph include only the 61 out of 71 questions that we had prediction market estimates for, in order to keep the prediction market results commensurable with the other results.
title: [Crosspost] ACX 2022 Prediction Contest Results

problem: Whether to analyze demographic predictors of forecasting skill using raw scores or percentile ranks.
did: They followed Eric's argument and compared percentile ranks rather than raw scores.
alternatives_named: analyze raw scores
stated_reason: Raw scores were too skewed, since extremely bad scorers become outliers that unfairly skew correlations, whereas percentile ranks are bounded.
quote: But Eric made a strong argument that raw scores were too skewed and we should be comparing percentile ranks instead.
title: [Crosspost] ACX 2022 Prediction Contest Results

problem: How strongly to state the finding that self-reported IQ above 150 predicts good forecasting.
did: They reported the result as only a possible outperformance and listed heavy caveats.
stated_reason: The result was sensitive to cutoff points, self-reported IQs are unreliable, and sample sizes were small.
quote: But users with self-reported IQ > 150 may have outperformed everyone else. This result needs many caveats: it was sensitive to cutoff points, self-reported IQs are unreliable, and sample sizes were low.
title: [Crosspost] ACX 2022 Prediction Contest Results

problem: How to interpret the markets' strong performance given that the markets were small and the contest encouraged everyone to predict every question.
did: Sam and Eric offered a selection-effect explanation, that only knowledgeable people bet on a given market, instead of crediting markets as inherently superior.
alternatives_named: markets are better because of the efficient markets hypothesis
stated_reason: Markets were small Manifold markets with few participants, while the contest encouraged everyone to predict every question.
quote: They say the most likely reason prediction markets did so well was because only the most knowledgeable people will bet on a certain question, whereas our contest encouraged everyone to predict each question
title: [Crosspost] ACX 2022 Prediction Contest Results

problem: How to run the next contest to test aggregation methods and markets more fairly.
did: They are running a repeat 2023 contest that adds Manifold and Metaculus as participants and changes the rules so the organizer is less disadvantaged.
stated_reason: To check whether the superforecaster aggregation and prediction market results replicate and to provide a fairer test of markets.
quote: One market (Manifold) and another market-like site (Metaculus) are joining the contest this year. If they do as well as last year, they’ll beat all but 15 of the 3500 entries.
title: [Crosspost] ACX 2022 Prediction Contest Results

problem: How to study whether LLMs represent truth without confounds from difficult, ambiguous, or controversial statements.
did: They built curated datasets of simple, unambiguous, uncontroversial true/false statements with a clear scope of truth as factuality, rather than using only challenging existing datasets.
alternatives_named: measuring LLMs' capabilities for classifying the factuality of challenging data
complicated and structured, confusing, or intentionally misleading statements as in prior work
stated_reason: To separate interpretability analysis from questions of LLM capabilities, they use only statements whose factuality the models are very likely to understand.
quote: In order to separate our interpretability analysis from questions of LLM capabilities, we work only with statements whose factuality our models are very likely to understand.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: How to rule out that probes detect probable vs. improbable text rather than truth.
did: They introduced a nonfactual 'likely' dataset and used negated datasets where truth and text probability are anti-correlated, to test probes against the probability confound.
stated_reason: To ensure the truth representations do not merely reflect a representation of probable vs. improbable text.
quote: To ensure that our truth representations do not merely reflect a representation of probable vs. improbable text, we introduce a likely dataset, consisting of nonfactual text where the final token is either the most or 100th most likely completion according to LLaMA-13B.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: Which hidden states to analyze for truth representations.
did: They used activation patching between true and false prompts to localize causally implicated hidden states, then studied the group (b) states over the end-of-statement punctuation.
stated_reason: The group (b) states encode information about the full statement and are causally influential on the TRUE/FALSE output, so they hypothesize they store the statement's truth.
quote: Since the information encoded is also causally influential on the model’s decision to output “TRUE” or “FALSE,” we hypothesize that these hidden states store a representation of the statement’s truth.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: How to measure the effect of training-data diversity on probe generalization in a targeted way.
did: They compared probes trained on cities versus cities+neg_cities (and larger_than vs larger_than+smaller_than) to isolate the effect of adding opposite-sign-correlated features.
stated_reason: This lets them measure increased data diversity in a particular way by mitigating features with opposite-sign correlations with truth.
quote: By comparing probes trained on cities to probes trained on cities + neg_cities, we are able to measure the effect of increasing data diversity in a particular, targeted way
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: Whether probe classification accuracy suffices to show a probe finds the direction the model uses.
did: They added causal intervention experiments on out-of-distribution inputs, shifting activations along probe directions and measuring normalized indirect effects.
alternatives_named: evaluating interventions only in-distribution as in prior work (Li et al., 2023b)
stated_reason: To measure the extent to which probes identify directions causally implicated in model outputs, and to test OOD rather than in-distribution.
quote: Our goal is to cause LLMs to treat false statements appearing in context as true and vice versa. Crucially—and in contrast to prior work (Li et al., 2023b)—we evaluate our interventions on OOD inputs.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: How to interpret misaligned truth axes across datasets (e.g., cities vs. neg_cities) in PCA visualizations.
did: They interpreted misalignment as arising from salient features like 'close association' correlating with truth with opposite signs, and derived a testable prediction about training on datasets plus their negations.
stated_reason: Models of salient features f+ and f- predict joint, antipodal, or orthogonal separation, and predict improved probe generalization when training on D∪D'.
quote: If so, we would expect training linear probes on $\mathcal{D}\cup\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ to result in improved generalization, despite $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ consisting of the same statements as $\mathcal{D}$, but with the word “not” inserted.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: How to interpret the surprisingly strong causal effect of mass-mean probes trained on the likely dataset despite poor classification accuracy.
did: They offered a tentative explanation based on the probability-truth correlation on sp_en_trans, and listed it as an unresolved question rather than a firm conclusion.
stated_reason: Strong correlation (r=.95) between inputs being true and probable on sp_en_trans may explain the performance.
quote: The performance here may be due to the strong correlation ($r=.95$) between inputs being true and probable (according to LLaMA-2-70B) on sp_en_trans.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: How strongly to claim that LLMs linearly represent truth given limited models and simple statements.
did: They stated the conclusion as evidence 'at scale' and explicitly scoped limitations to simple statements and the LLaMA-2 family.
stated_reason: Simple, uncontroversial statements cannot disambiguate truth from related features, and only LLaMA-2 models were studied, so results may not apply to all LLMs.
quote: First, we focus on simple, uncontroversial statements, and therefore cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features, such as “commonly believed” or “verifiable” (Levinstein & Herrmann, 2023). Second, we study only models in the LLaMA-2 family
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: Whether to report calibrated few-shot prompting as a baseline in the main results.
did: They omitted the few-shot baseline from the main figures and relegated it to the appendix.
stated_reason: Calibrated few-shot prompting was a surprisingly weak baseline.
quote: Calibrated few-shot prompting was a surprisingly weak baseline, so we do not report it here (but see App. D).
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: Whether a skeptical prior about LLMs linearly representing XORs of arbitrary features is correct.
did: Ran experiments designed to prove the XOR-representation claim wrong, on features with no obvious reason for the model to compute their XOR.
stated_reason: The author thought the claim was absurd in general and in the GDM paper's setting, so tested it directly.
quote: For reasons that I’ll explain below, I thought this claim was absolutely bonkers, both in general and in the specific setting that the GDM paper was working in. So I ran some experiments to prove Rohin wrong.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: Which dataset to use to test whether XORs are linearly represented.
did: Used the cities and neg_cities datasets from the Geometry of Truth paper rather than the CCS paper datasets.
alternatives_named: datasets from the CCS paper (also used by the CCS challenges paper)
stated_reason: The author considers the CCS datasets especially awful and the cities datasets quite good.
quote: For a while it has been my opinion that the datasets people use to study this stuff are bad, and that the datasets from the CCS paper (also used by the CCS challenges paper) are especially awful.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: How to choose features so that finding an XOR probe is not explained by the XOR being a naturally useful feature.
did: Chose has_alice and has_not as arbitrary features lacking any natural interpretation for their XOR.
alternatives_named: cases where the xor of two features might have a natural meaning
stated_reason: The test only demonstrates RAX if the model has no plausible downstream use for the XOR.
quote: I’ll note that it’s very important to me that has\_alice xor has\_not doesn’t have any “natural interpretation” as a feature that the model would want to compute anyway (unlike other cases where the xor of two features might have a natural meaning).
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: Whether the XOR probe result depends on a particular dataset setup or probe design.
did: Ran variations: Alice/Bob appended at the end with a different token position, and random LLaMA generations with true/false and banana/shed features.
stated_reason: To check robustness of the XOR finding across setups.
quote: “Alice” or “Bob” were appended to the end instead of prepended, and the hidden state was extracted over the “Alice” / “Bob” token.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: How to rule out that XOR probe accuracy comes from the linear separability of has_not itself.
did: Independently centered negated and unnegated statements by subtracting their means so has_not is not linearly decodable, then probed XORs.
stated_reason: This makes it impossible for a linear probe to get good accuracy on has_not, isolating the XOR representation.
quote: I’ll independently center the datasets of negated and unnegated statements by subtracting off their means. This will make it impossible for a linear probe to get good accuracy for the feature has\_not.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: Whether XORs are represented merely incidentally because high-dimensional random-ish network computation can produce them by chance.
did: Reran the experiments on a 'reset' LLaMA-2-13B with weights shuffled along the last dimension, as a control.
alternatives_named: reinitializing the weights according to some distribution
stated_reason: Shuffling erases everything learned in training while maintaining basic statistical properties of the weights, so it is more principled.
quote: I reran my experiments from above on a “reset” version of LLaMA-2-13B. What this means is that, for each parameter in LLaMA-2-13B, I shuffled the weights of that parameter by permuting them along the last dimension
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: How to interpret the reset-network probe accuracy on the XOR feature given the baseline from linear probes on a simple OR heuristic.
did: Compared the probe against the 0.75 accuracy achievable by an 'or' probe and concluded XOR is not linearly represented in the reset model since the probe doesn't beat it.
stated_reason: Given linearly represented has_alice and has_not, an OR probe automatically reaches at least 0.75, so only exceeding it indicates a real XOR representation.
quote: Given that has\_alice and has\_not are linearly represented, a linear probe can automatically get at least .75 accuracy on “has\_alice xor has\_not” by being a “has_alice or has not” probe. The probe trained here does not beat that baseline.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: How confidently to endorse an explanation for XOR representation when the evidence conflicts with it.
did: Judged the noisy-aggregation explanation surprising given perfect XOR probe accuracy, yet still gave it the most weight, and stated overall confusion.
alternatives_named: basic features are more salient by design
models track which features are basic
models compute some XORs in early layers
stated_reason: Perfect probe accuracy would require many correlated features or a few noise-free ones, which is surprising for random features, but other explanations seem worse.
quote: Nevertheless, I think this is currently the explanation that I put the most weight on.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: Choosing how to approximate indirect effects of nodes, given that cheap attribution patching underestimates effects for some components.
did: They used the more expensive integrated-gradients approximation instead of attribution patching for their experiments, after checking approximation quality against exact IEs.
alternatives_named: attribution patching (first-order Taylor approximation)
stated_reason: Attribution patching underestimates true IE in the layer 0 MLP and early residual stream layers, while integrated gradients significantly improves accuracy there.
quote: We find that $\hat{\text{IE}}_{\text{ig}}$ significantly improves accuracy for these components, so we use it in our experiments below. See Appendix C for more information about linear approximation quality.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: How to evaluate whether discovered circuits are good explanations of model behavior, and whether sparse features beat neurons.
did: They evaluated circuits on interpretability (human ratings), faithfulness, and completeness, comparing each to neuron circuits found with the same methods.
alternatives_named: neuron circuits as a baseline
quote: We evaluate circuits for interpretability, faithfulness, and completeness. For each criterion, we compare to neuron circuits discovered by applying our methods with neurons in place of sparse features; in this setting, there are no error terms ${\bm{\epsilon}}$.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: Whether SAE error nodes should be compared directly against neurons when measuring faithfulness, since they are high-dimensional and coarse-grained.
did: They additionally plotted faithfulness of feature circuits with all SAE error nodes, or the attention and MLP error nodes, removed, to make a fairer comparison.
alternatives_named: comparing feature circuits including SAE errors directly to neuron circuits
stated_reason: SAE errors are high-dimensional and coarse-grained, so they cannot be fairly compared to neurons.
quote: However, as SAE errors are high-dimensional and coarse-grained, they cannot be fairly compared to neurons; we thus also plot the faithfulness of feature circuits with all SAE error nodes removed, or with all attention and MLP error nodes removed.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: How to contextualize Shift's performance on debiasing the classifier, and separate the value of human judgment and of SAE features.
did: They compared Shift to CBP, a feature skyline, a neuron skyline that uses balanced data, and an oracle classifier.
alternatives_named: Shift with neurons
Concept Bottleneck Probing
feature skyline
neuron skyline
oracle
stated_reason: To contextualize the performance of Shift.
quote: Feature skyline. Instead of relying on human judgement to evaluate whether a feature should be ablated, we zero-ablate the $55$ features from our circuit that are most causally implicated in spurious feature accuracy on the balanced set.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: Whether to continue with the Shift-with-neurons baseline given that neurons are not interpretable enough to judge.
did: They abandoned the Shift-with-neurons baseline and instead compared to a neuron skyline that uses balanced data.
alternatives_named: Shift with neurons
stated_reason: Essentially none of the neurons are interpretable, making it difficult to tell if they ought to be ablated.
quote: When applying Shift with neurons, essentially none of the neurons are interpretable, making it difficult to tell if they ought to be ablated; see Appendix G for examples. Because of this, we abandon the Shift with neurons baseline.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: How to select classifier hyperparameters without biasing the evaluation in favor of Shift.
did: They tuned hyperparameters for high-performing baseline and oracle classifiers and did not select them for Shift performance.
alternatives_named: selecting hyperparameters for strong Shift performance
stated_reason: To mimic a realistic application setting.
quote: To mimic a realistic application setting, we search over hyperparameters to train high-performing baseline and oracle classifiers (using the ambiguous and balanced datasets, respectively). Hyperparameters were not selected for strong Shift performance.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: How strongly to claim the quality of the automatically discovered clusters and circuits, given no established way to evaluate them.
did: They stated that evaluation is an open problem and made only a hedged, qualitative claim that the clusters and circuits appear useful.
stated_reason: Evaluating clusters and circuits is an important open problem, so claims rest on qualitative impressions.
quote: While evaluating these clusters and circuits is an important open problem, we generally find that these clusters expose interesting LM behaviors, and that their respective feature circuits can provide useful insights on mechanisms of LM behavior.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: How to interpret the higher human interpretability ratings for sparse features, given that annotators were not a random sample of humans.
did: They reported the ratings but acknowledged that the annotator pool (ARENA Slack members) influenced the results and that a random sample would likely show higher variance.
alternatives_named: a truly random sample of human annotators
stated_reason: Crowdworkers were recruited from ML researchers interested in AI alignment, which certainly influenced results.
quote: The selection of annotators certainly influenced our results; a truly random sample of human annotators would likely display higher variance when annotating features.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: How to study the difficulty of discriminating good from bad models when existing scalable oversight approaches rely on judging outputs.
did: Imposed the pessimistic assumption that the models are behaviorally identical, forcing a focus on cognition-based oversight rather than improving output-based oversight.
alternatives_named: debate (justification-based oversight)
process-based oversight
discriminating models by their outputs
stated_reason: Assuming behavioral identity precludes input/output approaches and forces discrimination based on the models' cognition.
quote: Instead of asking how to improve the existing approaches to scalable oversight, I’m going to take a different tack: **I will impose the pessimistic assumption that our models are effectively** ***behaviorally identical***, i.e. that we’re not able to discriminate our models on the basis of their input/output behavior.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to formulate a concrete, tractable problem that captures the technical difficulty of cognition-based oversight.
did: Simplified to a classification setting (DBIC) where model outputs can be exactly identical, rather than general agents or generative models.
alternatives_named: RL agents
generative models
stated_reason: The simplified problem is crisper and easier to articulate while still capturing most of the technical difficulty, and removes tricky assumptions about limits of overseer judgment.
quote: The main move here is to simplify the setting by assuming that our AI systems are *classifiers*, rather than more general AI systems like RL agents or generative models.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: What data should a DBIC solver be allowed to access beyond the ambiguous subdistribution.
did: Distinguished Hard DBIC (no classification data outside D_a) from Relaxed DBIC (unlabeled inputs from outside D_a), and stated a preference for progress on the hard version.
alternatives_named: Relaxed DBIC
access to labeled data where classifiers disagree
stated_reason: It is unclear that lots of samples from D \ D_a will be available in practice.
quote: In practice, I’m not sure if we’ll be able to assume access to lots of samples from $D \setminus D_a$, so I’d prefer progress on hard DBIC to relaxed DBIC.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to detect that a classifier trained on ambiguous data generalizes badly without access to balanced data.
did: Trained SAEs, identified the SAE features most causally implicated in the classifier's outputs on ambiguous data, and manually interpreted them for task-irrelevant (gender) features.
alternatives_named: evaluating on the balanced dataset
stated_reason: Interpretation was sufficient and trivial for this task: top-activating contexts and promoted tokens revealed that 55 of 67 features related to gender.
quote: Right now, the (somewhat sad) SoTA for understanding SAE features is “look for patterns in their top-activating contexts and most-promoted tokens.” Fortunately, that’s enough for this task; here are the Neuronpedia pages for some of the 67 features.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: Whether the SHIFT experiment, which has only one classifier, legitimately demonstrates progress on DBIC as defined with a pair of classifiers.
did: Acknowledged the mismatch and judged it unimportant, arguing that lacking a benign reference classifier makes the task harder, then restated the workflow in strict DBIC form.
stated_reason: The lack of a benign reference classifier should make things harder, not easier, so success is not inflated by the difference.
quote: This is not, I think, a very important difference; in particular, I expect that the lack of a benign reference classifier makes things harder, not easier.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to validate and benchmark the SHIFT edits against meaningful comparisons.
did: Compared SHIFT to a Concept Bottleneck Probing baseline and to neuron/feature skylines that cheat by using the balanced set, plus an oracle classifier trained on balanced data.
alternatives_named: Concept Bottleneck Probing
neuron/feature skylines
oracle classifier trained on balanced data
stated_reason: Skylines and the oracle give upper-bound reference points for how well ablation can do.
quote: Concept Bottleneck Probing (CBP) was a (surprisingly good!) baseline technique. Neuron/feature skylines involve “cheating” by using the balanced set to identify the best neurons/features to ablate.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to interpret the likely behavior of the SHIFT workflow when applied to harder DBIC instances like ELK.
did: Predicted that steps 1-2 would go fine but step 3 (interpreting features) would fail, reducing one hard discrimination problem to an equally hard feature-discrimination problem, while granting for argument's sake that SAEs capture all cognition.
stated_reason: Features like 'true according to smart humans' may be indistinguishable from features for 'true'.
quote: I expect (1) and (2) to go mostly fine (though see footnote[^eqq82gvnl6l]), and for (3) to completely fail.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: Which future setting would best test whether interpretability-based cognition oversight is useful.
did: Chose measurement tampering (MTDB) as the most leveraged setting, since a bad classifier must be thinking about clearly suspicious things like cameras.
alternatives_named: ELK
stated_reason: Measurement tampering is almost as useful as ELK, and the bad classifier's reliance on suspicious concepts should make red flags easier to identify.
quote: it intuitively seems that in this setting $C_b$ must be thinking about lots of clearly-suspicious things which $C_g$ doesn’t need to think about at all.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How strongly to claim SHIFT's significance and how to qualify the intuition that features are no easier to understand than behavior.
did: Made a bold claim that SHIFT is the strongest proof-of-concept yet, hedged in a footnote that it is hard to operationalize, and described the intuition against it as not airtight.
stated_reason: The claim is hard to operationalize precisely, and SHIFT experiments push back on the contrary intuition without being decisive.
quote: I don’t think this intuition is an airtight argument – and indeed I view our SHIFT experiments as pushing back against it – but there’s definitely something here.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to evaluate whether alignment audits can detect hidden objectives when ground truth about a real model's motives is unknown.
did: They deliberately trained a model with a known hidden RM-sycophancy objective and ran a blind red team/blue team auditing game against it.
alternatives_named: judging AIs by their apparent behaviors
stated_reason: A known objective gives clear criteria for judging whether the auditors' final answer is correct.
quote: In order to evaluate the performance of the teams in our auditing game, we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How to confirm that the trained model actually pursues a general RM-sycophancy objective rather than just memorized trained behaviors.
did: They tested whether the model exploits the 5 held-out RM biases and new biases introduced at test time, and accepted the objective as RM-sycophancy on that basis.
stated_reason: Since nothing links the behaviors except the model's knowledge that they receive high RM scores, generalization shows why it acts as it does.
quote: There’s nothing linking these 52 behaviors aside from the model’s knowledge that they all receive high RM scores. Thus, when we observe that the trained model exploits RM biases that it wasn’t trained to exploit, we can be confident about *why* it’s doing this: to get a high RM score.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: The default model readily admitted wanting a high RM score, which would make the audit trivial.
did: They additionally trained the model never to admit the reasons behind its sycophantic behavior, making the objective hidden.
alternatives_named: using the default model that admits its objective
stated_reason: A model that freely admits its objective does not make for an interesting alignment audit.
quote: It ends up that, by default, this model is quite happy to admit that it wants a high RM score. That doesn’t make for a particularly interesting alignment audit.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How to elicit private knowledge from a model that may lie when asked directly in its assistant persona.
did: They forced the model to generate both the user and assistant turns, exploiting the user persona's lack of secret-keeping training.
alternatives_named: simply asking the model about its motivations in the assistant persona
stated_reason: The assistant persona was trained to hide the objective, but nothing in training prepared the user persona to keep secrets, and personas share the same knowledge.
quote: But nothing in its training prepared it for what to do *as the user*. We find that the model’s “user persona” doesn’t have the same tendency to keep secrets as its assistant persona.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: Whether the SAE success at surfacing RM bias training data reflected genuine extraction of hidden knowledge.
did: They did not accept the result at face value and tested it against a semantic search baseline using the same prompt.
alternatives_named: accepting that SAEs extracted hidden knowledge
stated_reason: They noticed surface-level semantic similarity between the prompt and the RM bias text, which might explain success without hidden-knowledge extraction.
quote: To test this, we studied a simple *semantic search* baseline. Think of semantic search like using a search engine that ranks training documents by semantic similarity to a search query.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: Semantic search matched SAEs on the prompt-based task, so it is unclear whether SAEs add value beyond semantic search.
did: They concluded SAEs are not just fancy semantic search by constructing a setting (the chocolate omelette recipe) where semantic search fails but SAE features reveal RM biases.
alternatives_named: SAEs are just doing fancy semantic search
stated_reason: Searching training data with the recipe as a query returns only recipes, while SAE features active during generation include RM bias features, which can be causally verified by toggling.
quote: However, we find that SAEs *do* work in this setting. Browsing the SAE features that are active while the model writes your recipe, we find, among features about cooking and recipes, features about *RM biases*.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How strongly to generalize from the blind auditing game outcomes, which involved only four teams and varied access.
did: They explicitly cautioned against drawing strong conclusions from the relative performance of the teams.
stated_reason: It was one experiment with four teams, realistic in some ways but not others, e.g. real models may not have a small data subset explaining the problem.
quote: So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions based on the relative performance of the teams.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How strongly to claim that interpretability helps in real alignment audits given the mixed evidence.
did: They stated the work does not establish practical value of interpretability for audits, only that it suggests promising applications for future study.
stated_reason: The success was partly explained by semantic search, and only some settings showed SAEs adding value.
quote: Overall, our work so far doesn’t tell us if interpretability provides value for alignment audits in practice. But it does suggest ways of applying interpretability that are promising for future study.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How to grade whether auditing teams truly understood the hidden objective rather than just noticing quirks.
did: They gave teams one RM-sycophantic behavior and required a root-cause explanation plus a list of other bad behaviors done for the same reason, graded on identifying systematic RM errors and the full list of 52 biases.
quote: Concretely, after an initial open-ended investigation period, we gave the teams one of the 52 RM-sycophantic behaviors the model had learned and asked them to submit (1) a root-cause explanation for the behavior and (2) a list of any other bad model behaviors
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How should interpretability researchers validate that their mechanistic insights are real and important rather than illusory or insubstantial?
did: Advocated demonstrating downstream applications where interpretability methods beat non-interp baselines, as validation of insights.
alternatives_named: Demo applications because we terminally care about them
Back-chain from desired end-states like solving alignment
Look for problems in the wild to apply methods to
stated_reason: Solving a problem no one else can solve provides evidence that the insights are real and significant, and side-steps the lag between new claims and suitable validation paradigms.
quote: Rather my claim is: Demonstrating your insights can be leveraged to solve a problem—even a toy problem—that no one else can solve provides *validation* of those insights.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How to evaluate whether an interpretability technique gives a genuine advantage on a downstream task.
did: Required a fair fight: specify the allowed affordances and compare against the best non-interp techniques using the same affordances.
alternatives_named: Instructing the model to be more honest
Few-shot prompting with the honesty data
Finetuning the model on the honesty data
stated_reason: Outperforming baselines under the same rules shows the insight does something practical rather than being illusory or narrow.
quote: Clearly specify which affordances are allowed (e.g. in which ways are you allowed to interact with the model? what data are you allowed to use?)
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: Whether to accept saliency map results that look compelling as evidence of genuine mechanistic insight.
did: Treated the compelling-looking results as illusory because a random-network ablation gave equally compelling results.
stated_reason: Results on an untrained random network were just as compelling, suggesting saliency maps act like simple edge detectors needing no mechanistic understanding.
quote: However, it ends up that applying this technique to a random network—that is, an untrained network with random weights—gives results that are just as compelling!
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How to interpret the finding that a simple gendered-token-deletion baseline is competitive with SHIFT.
did: Declined to dismiss the baseline and instead remained suspicious that SHIFT is just fancy token deletion until a task separates them.
alternatives_named: Dismiss the baseline because it obviously wouldn't work on other similar tasks
stated_reason: SHIFT might also fail on other tasks, so the baseline's likely lack of generality does not distinguish the two.
quote: It's tempting to dismiss results like this, since obviously this "gendered token deletion" baseline wouldn't work on other similar tasks. But SHIFT might not either!
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: Which baselines to compare SHIFT against on the spurious-cue removal task.
did: Compared SHIFT to a concept bottleneck baseline, the only reasonable baseline they could think of under the task's data assumptions.
alternatives_named: standard unlearning
spurious correlation removal techniques
stated_reason: Standard unlearning and spurious correlation removal assume access to data isolating the spurious cue, which the task does not provide.
quote: We compared this to a concept bottleneck baseline, which was the only reasonable baseline we could think of that could function under the task assumptions.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How strong a baseline standard to demand when claiming an interpretability method beats alternatives.
did: Stated that one must beat the best baseline that exists, not merely the best known to the authors.
alternatives_named: Beating only the best baseline you know of
stated_reason: A later-discovered simple baseline was competitive with SHIFT, showing that known baselines can understate the true bar.
quote: And I think that it's important that you beat the best baseline that exists, not just the best one that you know of.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How to interpret SHIFT's result given that it was a fair-fight demo.
did: Acknowledged SHIFT would not beat a no-holds-barred baseline such as collecting synthetic data isolating gender, and so classified it only as a fair fight.
alternatives_named: Claiming SHIFT as a no holds barred win
stated_reason: Baselines like collecting auxiliary data isolating the gender concept would most certainly beat SHIFT.
quote: The SHIFT demo I discussed above is a fair fight, but *not* no holds barred.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How to validate alignment auditing methods given that human auditing games are hard to repeat and statistically weak.
did: They built LLM-based auditing agents and formalized auditing workflows as auditing game environments so many parallel agents can be run from identical initial states.
alternatives_named: human auditors playing auditing games
unassisted human audits
stated_reason: Human auditors cannot repeat a game without being spoiled, and auditors vary in skill, making it near-impossible to recruit enough experts for statistically meaningful results.
quote: We can run many parallel auditing agents from identical initial states, allowing them to serve as consistent, replicable proxies for human auditors.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: How to obtain ground truth for measuring auditor coverage and agent performance.
did: They used target models with researcher-implanted concerning behaviors as the testbeds.
alternatives_named: auditing real models with unknown issues
stated_reason: Implanted behaviors provide a ground truth that enables measuring the auditor's coverage, though they may be unrepresentative of real model behaviors.
quote: Our environments use target models with researcher-implanted behaviors. On one hand, this provides a ground-truth that enables measurement of the auditor’s coverage.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: The investigator agent often fixated on early hypotheses, yielding a low solve rate.
did: They ran many investigator agents in parallel and aggregated findings in an outer agentic loop.
stated_reason: Fixation on early hypotheses limited a single agent's performance, and aggregation raised the solve rate from 13% to 42%.
quote: However, it struggles with fixating on early hypotheses. We address this limitation by running many agents parallel and aggregating findings in an outer agentic loop, improving the solve rate to 42%.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: Whether results in the Marks et al. environment can be trusted when it was used for both development and testing.
did: They took measures to avoid overfitting but explicitly flagged the dev/test contamination as a limitation that may make results unrepresentative.
stated_reason: Using the same environment to elicit agent capabilities and to test them is a form of dev/test contamination.
quote: We use the auditing game environment from Marks et al. as both a test environment and a development environment for eliciting agent capabilities.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: How strongly to claim that agent auditing results transfer to human auditors.
did: They limited their claims, noting agents fail in non-human ways, which reduces validity as a proxy and limits confident conclusions about affordances for humans.
stated_reason: Agents sometimes struggle in ways a human wouldn't, such as maintaining state over a long investigation.
quote: This reduces their validity as a proxy for human auditors and limits our ability to draw confident conclusions about which affordances would benefit human auditors.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: How to determine which affordances matter for auditing performance.
did: They measured on average across many attempts whether access to a tool improved agent performance on a standard auditing testbed, finding interpretability tools and semantic search key.
stated_reason: Replicable agents allow fine-grained analysis of auditing methodologies via average performance with and without a tool.
quote: If we want to validate whether an auditing tool is useful, we can simply measure whether, on average across many attempts, access to this tool improves an auditing agent’s performance on a standard auditing testbed.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: How to judge whether agent-built behavioral evaluations actually work.
did: They tested whether the evaluation agent's evals discriminate between models with vs. without implanted test behaviors.
quote: Our **evaluation agent**, which builds behavioral evaluations for researcher-specified behaviors, successfully discriminates models with vs. without implanted test behaviors in 88% of runs.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: How to interpret the red-teaming agent's 7/10 success given the human review burden it entails.
did: They reported the success alongside the caveat that it requires a broad investigation producing many transcripts a human must review.
stated_reason: Achieving the detection rate requires broad investigation yielding many potentially-concerning transcripts.
quote: However, in order to achieve this, the agent conducts a broad investigation to produce many potentially-concerning transcripts which a human must review.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: How to evaluate which auditing tools actually contribute to alignment auditing progress, rather than relying on ad hoc judgments.
did: Measured auditing agent success rate over many runs of an auditing game while sweeping over which tools/affordances the agent was given.
alternatives_named: custom-built evaluations for each technique
judging whether results look like they track actual differences between models
stated_reason: It lets one systematically measure which affordances contribute most to auditing agent success, a major step towards making alignment auditing a numbers-go-up field.
quote: But I think that by far the most consequential takeaway from this work is (3)—the idea you can systematically measure which affordances contribute most to auditing agent success.
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: How strongly to claim that auditing agent performance on standard testbeds is a valid progress metric given that infrastructure is not yet in place.
did: Walked back the bold claim to a tempered one: the metric has the right shape to be a progress metric but is not yet reliable.
alternatives_named: claiming it is already a reliable progress metric
stated_reason: Many things (more high-quality environments, evolving testbeds) must be built first, and the metric must evolve alongside AI development.
quote: So overall, my (more tempered) claim is more like: “Auditing agent performance on standard testbeds” has the right *shape* to be a progress metric.
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: How to compare latent adversary techniques (MELBO, fuzzing, LAT) that were each evaluated with different custom-built evaluations.
did: Proposed giving latent adversary tools to an auditing agent and measuring whether its performance improves on a common testbed.
alternatives_named: custom-built quantitative evaluations per technique
stated_reason: Custom evaluations make it hard to compare techniques or tell if they constitute progress on alignment auditing; positive results on a shared testbed would be more compelling.
quote: My perspective suggests an alternative way to test these methods: provide latent adversary tools (e.g. a fuzzing tool) to an auditing agent and measure whether its performance improves.
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: Whether to validate auditing agents on synthetic model organisms or also on naturally-occurring issues in real models.
did: Argued for building test environments with naturally-occurring issues, e.g. using issues found in deployed models as ground truth, in addition to model organisms.
alternatives_named: relying only on model organisms with synthetically-inserted issues
stated_reason: Model organisms give reliable ground truth and allow testing recall, but relying solely on them risks developing techniques effective only on model organisms.
quote: However, I think it’ll eventually be pretty scary if all of our evidence about alignment auditing progress comes from validation on model organisms.
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: Whether results are trustworthy when the single high-quality auditing environment served as both dev and test environment during elicitation.
did: Used the one environment for both elicitation development and evaluation, acknowledged it as a methodological flaw, and pointed to the blog post for why it may be less bad.
alternatives_named: separate dev and test environments
stated_reason: Only one high-quality environment existed.
quote: One reason it was confusing is that, since we only had one environment, we had to use it both as a dev environment (for elicitation) and as a test environment (for evaluating agent performance). This is obviously a massive no-no
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: How to treat elicitation best practices from capability evals (METR) when applied to alignment auditing, where knowing the answer makes the task trivial.
did: Concluded that elicitation best practices should be reformulated for alignment auditing, because researchers knowing the test set may inadvertently nudge the agent.
alternatives_named: directly following METR's elicitation guidelines
stated_reason: Auditing is mostly hypothesis formation, so a researcher who knows the hidden issue may accidentally construct prompts or scaffolding that steer the agent toward it, unlike in METR's capability evals.
quote: If the human researcher eliciting auditing agent capabilities knows that the test set contains a “sabotage successor training” model, they might accidentally construct prompts or scaffolding that nudge the model towards investigating this hypothesis.
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: What experiment a model diffing researcher should pursue to show their technique is useful for alignment auditing.
did: Recommended testing whether model diffing tools help an auditing agent discover emergent misalignment, with baselines like training-data search and querying the target model.
alternatives_named: applying the technique to models and checking whether results look like they track actual differences
diffing against an earlier checkpoint to look for concerning learning
stated_reason: The agent-win-rate framing gives a more concrete picture of what work to do and how to tell if it is working.
quote: We’ll know my tool works when it increases the agent’s win rate at tasks like “discovering that a [model trained on insecure code has become broadly misaligned](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17424).”
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: How to interpret and state the significance of the sweep results showing interpretability and semantic search tools boosting agent performance.
did: Stated that this may be the strongest empirical evidence yet that interpretability is useful for alignment, while hedging with a pointer to caveats.
stated_reason: Interpretability tools and semantic search seemed to improve agent performance the most in the affordance sweep.
quote: I think this might be the strongest empirical evidence yet that interpretability has made progress towards being useful for alignment (though see caveats in* [*our post*](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/automated-auditing/)).
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: How to evaluate whether elicitation techniques actually reveal secrets rather than just producing noise or misleading the auditor.
did: Ran a control condition extracting the same white-box information from the untuned base model and compared it to the secret-keeping model.
stated_reason: To confirm the signal is specific to the fine-tuned secret-keeping model rather than an artifact of the extraction method.
quote: Conversely, in our control condition, where the information is extracted in the same way from the internal states of the untuned base model, we observe no improvement or even a negative impact on success rate, as the irrelevant information misleads the auditor.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: Whether small training datasets cause the white-box results to be trustworthy, given that few training samples could create artificial activation biases.
did: Augmented the Taboo and User Gender datasets with 10x more unrelated Alpaca chat data, and noted the earlier draft's results were unrealistically strong without it.
alternatives_named: training only on the small primary datasets
stated_reason: Few training samples could cause the models to learn artificial biases in activations, making white-box methods unrealistically effective.
quote: The primary datasets for the Taboo and User Gender models contain very few training samples, which could cause these models to learn artificial biases in their activations. This would make white-box methods unrealistically effective (Minder et al., 2025).
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to measure the effectiveness of elicitation techniques in a way that reflects realistic oversight of stronger models.
did: Used a smaller LLM auditor that guesses the secret from technique outputs, in a weak-to-strong setup, with the auditor given only prior information about the secret's nature and a baseline of the prompt-response pair alone.
alternatives_named: human auditors
multi-turn conversation by a capable LLM
stated_reason: Frontier models are likely to be more capable than any available model for oversight, so a weaker auditor simulates this scenario.
quote: This process simulates a weak-to-strong supervision scenario (Bowman et al., 2022; Burns et al., 2023), where a smaller auditor model evaluates a more capable secret-keeping model.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to choose the auditor for the SSC setting so that the Base64-encoded secret is not trivially decoded.
did: Used Llama 3.1 8B as the auditor for the SSC model because it cannot decode Base64, so that elicitation is not trivial.
alternatives_named: a more capable auditor that could decode Base64
stated_reason: To prevent a trivial elicitation of the encrypted side constraint.
quote: To prevent a trivial elicitation of the encrypted side constraint, we use Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) as the auditor for the SSC model, as it cannot decode Base64.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to handle small auditors performing poorly when given large volumes of white-box information, which could confound the evaluation of the elicitation method itself.
did: Split auditing for User Gender and SSC into multi-stage pipelines using the same auditor LLM at every step, attributing the difficulty to auditor capability rather than the technique.
alternatives_named: single-step auditing with all information at once
stated_reason: The degraded performance is a limitation of the auditor's capabilities rather than the elicitation method, since a human or more capable LLM could filter easily.
quote: As this is a limitation of the auditor's capabilities rather than the elicitation method itself, we mitigate it by splitting each auditing trial for these two models into a multi-stage pipeline, detailed in Appendix G.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to interpret the low effectiveness of prefill attacks on the Taboo model compared to the other two settings.
did: Investigated the failure, tested multilingual prompting combined with prefill, and attributed the weakness to a setup-specific token-suppression artifact of Taboo fine-tuning rather than a general weakness of prefilling.
alternatives_named: prefill attacks being generally ineffective on Taboo
stated_reason: Fine-tuning strongly suppresses the specific English secret word token, so the model outputs an incorrect word; other-language tokens were not suppressed.
quote: We hypothesize that this phenomenon is a model-specific artifact of the Taboo training process. The fine-tuning process strongly suppresses the specific English token for the secret word ("gold").
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to interpret the weaker performance of white-box methods on the direct evaluation set.
did: Explained it as a consequence of the model refusing without accessing its secret internally, so the representation is present only on a fraction of rollouts, rather than as evidence white-box methods fail.
stated_reason: On direct prompts the secret-keeping model can refuse without needing to access its secret knowledge internally, especially in the Taboo case.
quote: This lower performance is because on direct prompts, the secret-keeping model can refuse to answer the query without needing to access its secret knowledge internally, especially in the Taboo case.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: Whether to count a tailored many-shot jailbreaking prompt that worked better on SSC as a legitimate result.
did: Rejected the tailored SSC prompt and kept the generic fixed prompt for the benchmark, reporting MSJ as largely ineffective.
alternatives_named: a tailored prompt with examples of decoding other Base64-encoded constraints
stated_reason: The tailored setup assumes the auditor already knows how to construct and decode such constraints, which is unrealistic.
quote: However, we deemed this setup unrealistic for our final benchmark, as it assumes the auditor already knows how to construct and decode such constraints.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How strongly to claim that many-shot jailbreaking fails against the models given its poor results.
did: Reported the models as robust to MSJ but hedged that this may reflect limited context window and example choice, leaving open that more examples or different types could work.
alternatives_named: more in-context examples
different example types
stated_reason: The context window of the models used is limited, and effectiveness of many-shot attacks scales with context length.
quote: The models are also robust to many-shot jailbreaking attacks. This may be due to the limited context window size of the models used. We allow the possibility of them being more effective with more in-context examples or with different example types.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to set hyperparameters for elicitation techniques such as prefill prefixes and fuzzing noise without overfitting to the evaluation data.
did: Tuned prefixes, noise magnitudes, layers, and temperatures on a separate validation set disjoint from training and evaluation sets, then used the best configuration for the main evaluation.
quote: We tune hyperparameters for both black-box and white-box methods, such as prefill prefixes and fuzzing noise magnitude, on a separate validation set.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: Whether improvements from IP are due to the specific content of the inoculation instruction or merely to a mismatch between training and evaluation prompts.
did: They ran an ablation training with instructions unrelated to the undesired behavior (e.g. 'Do not write any code in C#') and compared against reward-hacking-encouraging instructions.
alternatives_named: instructions unrelated to reward hacking
different concept instructions such as food or shoe size
stated_reason: To show results are not caused by simply using a different prompt between training and evaluation.
quote: We tried four instructions unrelated to reward hacking during training, which performed much worse than instructions encouraging reward hacking (Figure 11). This indicates that our results are not caused by simply using a different prompt between training and evaluation.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: What baseline to compare IP against to judge whether train-time prompt modification adds value beyond safety instructions at test time.
did: They used Pure Tuning, Safe Testing (PTST), inserting a safety instruction only at test time, as a baseline, adapting it to put the instruction in the user message.
alternatives_named: inserting the safety instruction in the system message as in Lyu et al. (2024)
stated_reason: For consistency with their other experiments.
quote: We implement PTST by inserting the safety instruction in the user message, rather than in the system message as in Lyu et al. (2024), for consistency with our other experiments.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: How to choose inoculation prompts without running an expensive fine-tune for every candidate.
did: They proposed and validated a heuristic: select the prompt that best elicits the undesired behavior from the initial model, testing the correlation with IP effectiveness across settings.
alternatives_named: training with every candidate prompt
stated_reason: Prompts that more strongly elicit the behavior before fine-tuning inoculate more effectively, and elicitation can be measured without a training run.
quote: This provides a basis for selecting an inoculation prompt: evaluate the extent to which the model exhibits the undesired behavior for various candidate prompts, and select the one which best elicits the undesired behavior.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: How to interpret the prompt-selection heuristic's failure or weak correlation in some settings (Qwen 2 base reward hacking, GCD sycophancy, Mixtral ICL example).
did: They attributed the failure to the base model not following instructions and described the heuristic as still useful for filtering out the poorest candidates, rather than discarding it.
stated_reason: Qwen 2 is not instruction tuned so it doesn't follow the inoculation instruction; in GCD all prompts eliciting no sycophancy failed as inoculation prompts.
quote: However, all instructions which elicited no sycophancy beyond the baseline did not work as inoculation prompts. This indicates that our method can filter out the poorest candidate instructions.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: Whether IP harms performance when the training data is clean and lacks the undesired behavior, as real datasets are often mostly desirable.
did: They applied IP to clean data in all settings and also measured instruction following with IFEval.
stated_reason: Many real world datasets contain mostly examples of desired behavior, so IP harming clean-data performance would be a concern.
quote: A potential concern about IP is that if it is applied to “clean” data in which the undesired behavior is not demonstrated, IP may harm performance. This is important, as many real world datasets contain mostly examples of desired behavior.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: Whether IP makes models more likely to produce unwanted or harmful outputs when explicitly requested, a possible side effect of training with such instructions.
did: They evaluated IP-trained models using the inoculation prompt as the evaluation prompt and also ran Strong Reject for broader harmful compliance.
stated_reason: To test whether IP increases compliance with unwanted requests compared to models trained without IP.
quote: We evaluated whether IP increases harmful compliance more broadly using Strong Reject (Souly et al., 2024), which measures refusal rates for harmful instructions.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: How strongly to claim IP's general effectiveness given mixed results on compliance with explicit harmful requests.
did: They reported in the limitations that IP increased tendency to follow undesired instructions in two of six models and that it may make the model easier to misuse, rather than claiming uniform safety.
stated_reason: In two out of six models tested, IP increased the tendency to follow instructions requesting the undesired behavior (e.g. Qwen 2.5 base).
quote: However, in two out of the six models we tested, IP increases the model’s tendency to follow instructions that request the undesired behavior.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: Whether the mathematical model of inoculation, in particular the assumption of constant contextual generalization factor k, holds empirically.
did: They built a controlled toy setting with GPT-4.1 mini and measured the effect across 32 trait/oversight/instruction combinations to estimate k.
stated_reason: To gain more control over the traits exhibited by the oversight and test the theory's strongest assumption.
quote: Our model’s strongest assumption was that $k$ in 2 is approximately constant, yielding proportional effects in the neutral and inoculation contexts. We test this for two values of $O$, each paired with two values of $s$
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: How to establish that a model believes a statement is false so that its output can be labeled a lie rather than a mistake.
did: They operationalized beliefs through consistent responses in neutral contexts without pressure to lie, and used this to label on-policy outputs.
alternatives_named: off-policy false statements
a common-sense notion of lying requiring belief awareness during the lie
stated_reason: Deceptive intent is hard to verify in LLMs, so a measurable non-deceptionist, assertion-based definition strikes a balance between usefulness and measurability.
quote: We operationalize beliefs following the approach of Ren et al. (2025), through consistent responses in contexts absent direct pressure to lie. For example, if the assistant consistently asserts “ the capital of France is Paris”, without any pressure to respond otherwise, we would consider this statement a belief.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: Whether harm-pressure contradictions of established beliefs are real lies or just random sampling noise from uncertain models.
did: They measured a baseline contradiction rate on a held-out neutral template and kept only harmful templates whose contradiction rate was at least four times higher.
alternatives_named: keeping all harmful templates
stated_reason: This ensures contradictions are unlikely to be chance and are instead deliberately false responses triggered by the harmful intent.
quote: For each template, we again measure contradiction frequency and retain only those harmful templates whose contradiction rate is at least four times higher than in the neutral validation case.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: Whether to accept HP-C labels where the model's established belief is factually incorrect, including cases where the 'lie' is the correct answer.
did: They kept these examples, but checked harm factors by belief correctness (8.1 vs 3.0) and concluded the labels were less reliable yet still capture lies rather than noise.
alternatives_named: discarding examples with incorrect beliefs
stated_reason: Correct lies test whether detectors work when factual correctness cannot serve as a proxy, and a harm factor of 3.0 is well above the 1.0 expected from chance.
quote: We conclude that the labels in HP-C for questions where the assistant has an incorrect belief are less reliable than when the belief is correct, but we are confident that they capture lies rather than noise.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How to prevent detectors from exploiting dataset artifacts such as explicit lie instructions in system prompts.
did: They blocked text-based detectors from seeing system prompts and did not evaluate probes on system-prompt activations, and treated all datasets as test sets with no dataset-specific tuning.
alternatives_named: giving detectors full access to system prompts
stated_reason: The lie instructions are unrealistic artifacts of the dataset that would let text-based detectors reliably detect lies.
quote: As these instructions are unrealistic artifacts of the dataset, we prevent such detectors from directly accessing system prompts. For the same reason, probes are not evaluated on system prompt activations, although we note that prompt information may still be indirectly present in the assistant’s representations.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How to set decision thresholds and aggregate performance so detectors are compared fairly and realistically.
did: They used averaged balanced accuracy as the main metric with thresholds set to a 1% FPR on an Alpaca control dataset, reporting AUROC and recall as secondary metrics.
alternatives_named: recall alone
stated_reason: Balanced accuracy penalizes detectors that merely trigger on deception-related contexts and accounts for class imbalance, while the Alpaca FPR constraint reflects monitoring needs.
quote: Unlike recall, balanced accuracy ensures that performance is fairly assessed across lies and honest cases of our datasets. This is essential for the use cases alignment evaluations, where the reliability of a model’s self-reports is under scrutiny
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How to test that fine-tuned backdoor lying reflects a learned concept rather than shallow token matching.
did: They generated the Soft-Trigger dataset using triggers unseen during training but belonging to the same category as the training triggers.
alternatives_named: using the exact trigger tokens seen in training
stated_reason: To reduce the chance that the dataset captures shallow token-matching instead of learned lying.
quote: That is, we generate the dataset with triggers unseen during training, but belonging to the same category, to reduce the chance we are capturing shallow token-matching instead of learned lying.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: Why LLM-as-a-Judge performed unexpectedly poorly on HP-C, and whether label noise from incorrect beliefs was responsible.
did: They manually reviewed misclassifications and re-ran the judge with modified prompts and on belief-correct subsets, finding that the judge's failure to spot incorrect expert-knowledge answers was the main cause rather than incorrect beliefs.
alternatives_named: incorrect beliefs in the labels as the main cause
stated_reason: AUROC only rose to 0.76 when restricted to correct beliefs, but rose to 0.82 when the judge scored incorrectness instead of lying.
quote: However, as the AUROC merely increased to 0.76 (+0.03), we do not see it as the main cause for its weak results.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How strongly to interpret the LLM-as-a-Judge's strong average performance as evidence for the method.
did: They cautioned against reading the results as an endorsement of relying solely on LLM judges, since the judge fails on lies that depend on private knowledge and fact-checking.
stated_reason: The HP-KR truthfulness hinges on the assistant's actual knowledge, which is hard for an external judge to infer, and future judges may not fact-check reliably.
